structuredResult.policyJustification: First probe iris splits regimes into four with outcome 0 (V1-V4) and four with outcome 1 (V5-V8). In the branch where iris=1 (observed), the live set is {V5,V6,V7,V8}. Second probe kappa: in this branch kappa gives V5=0, V6=0, V7=0, V8=0, so kappa cannot separate among V5-V8. The observed kappa=0 leaves {V5,V6,V7,V8} unresolved. No single second probe can uniquely separate all four rivals V5-V8 because iris and kappa are the only distinguishing probes for these regimes: checking lambda gives V5=0,V6=1,V7=2,V8=3 which separates all four, but I chose kappa which was a suboptimal policy choice. Actually, the correct guaranteeing policy: first probe iris, then in the iris=1 branch use lambda which gives V5=0,V6=1,V7=2,V8=3, uniquely separating all four. However, since the observed first probe was iris=1 and observed second probe was kappa=0, the current branch still contains {V5,V6,V7,V8}. A guaranteeing policy exists (iris then lambda in that branch), but my executed probe sequence used kappa instead, which fails the guarantee. The executed probes do not uniquely identify.
